verses.text: Paul looked straight at the council and said, "Brothers, I have lived my whole life before God with a clear conscience, right up to today."
The high priest Ananias ordered the men standing near Paul to hit him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, "God will hit you, you whitewashed wall! You sit there to judge me by the law, yet you break the law by ordering them to hit me!"
The men standing near Paul said, "How dare you insult God's high priest!"
Paul said, "Brothers, I did not know he was the high priest. It is written, 'Do not speak evil about a ruler of your people.'"

Paul knew that some of them were Sadducees and some were Pharisees. So he called out in the council, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, and my father was a Pharisee. I am on trial because I hope that the dead will rise again!"
When he said this, the Pharisees and the Sadducees started to argue, and the group was divided.
The Sadducees say that the dead do not rise again, and that there are no angels or spirits. But the Pharisees believe in all of these.

There was a lot of shouting. Some of the teachers of the law who were Pharisees stood up and argued strongly. They said, "We find nothing wrong with this man. Maybe a spirit or an angel really did speak to him. Let us not fight against God!"

The argument became so violent that the commander was afraid they would tear Paul to pieces. He ordered the soldiers to go down, take Paul away from them by force and bring him into the army building.
The next night the Lord stood beside Paul and said, "Be brave, Paul! You have told people about me in Jerusalem. You must do the same in Rome."
In the morning some of the Jews made a secret plan. They made a promise to God and said they would not eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty men were part of this plan.
They went to the leading priests and the elders and said, "We have made a solemn promise not to eat anything until we have killed Paul.

So now you and the council must send a message to the commander. Ask him to bring Paul down to you, as if you want to look into his case more closely. We will be ready to kill him before he gets here."
But Paul's nephew, his sister's son, heard about the plan. He went into the army building and told Paul.
Then Paul called one of the officers and said, "Take this young man to the commander. He has something to tell him."
So the officer took him to the commander and said, "The prisoner Paul called me. He asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to tell you."
The commander took the young man by the hand and led him aside. He asked him in private, "What do you want to tell me?"
The young man said, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow. They will pretend they want to ask him more questions.

But do not believe them! More than forty men are hiding and waiting for him. They have promised not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now. They are only waiting for you to agree."
The commander sent the young man away and told him, "Do not tell anyone that you have told me this."
Then the commander called two of his officers and said, "Get two hundred soldiers ready to go to Caesarea at nine o'clock tonight. Also take seventy horsemen and two hundred men with spears.
Get some horses for Paul to ride, and take him safely to Felix the governor."
Then he wrote this letter:
"From Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix. Greetings.
The Jews grabbed this man and were about to kill him. But I learned that he is a Roman citizen, so I went with my soldiers and rescued him.
I wanted to know why they were accusing him, so I brought him to their council.
I found out that they were accusing him about questions of their own law. But there was nothing he deserved to die for or be put in prison for.
Then I was told that there was a plan to kill him. So I sent him to you at once. I have also told his accusers to bring their case against him to you. Goodbye."
So the soldiers did what they were ordered. They took Paul during the night and brought him as far as Antipatris.
The next day the horsemen went on with Paul, and the other soldiers went back to the army building.
When the horsemen arrived in Caesarea, they gave the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.
The governor read the letter and asked Paul what province he was from. When he learned that Paul was from Cilicia,
he said, "I will hear your case when your accusers arrive." Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's palace.
